passages.title: Gantt chart - Wikipedia
passages.text: Gantt chart A Gantt chart is a bar chart that illustrates a project schedule used in project management.[1] It was designed and popularized by Henry Gantt c. 1910–1915.[2][3] Modern Gantt charts also show the dependency relationships between activities and the current schedule status. Definition [edit] A Gantt chart is a type of bar chart[4][5] that illustrates a project schedule.[6] This chart lists the tasks to be performed on the vertical axis, and time intervals on the horizontal axis.[4][7] The width of the horizontal bars in the graph shows the duration of each activity.[7][8] Gantt charts illustrate the start and finish dates of the terminal elements and summary elements of a project.[1] Terminal elements and summary elements constitute the work breakdown structure of the project. Modern Gantt charts also show the dependency (i.e., precedence network) relationships between activities. Gantt charts can be used to show current schedule status using percent-complete shadings and a vertical "TODAY" line. Gantt charts are sometimes equated with bar charts.[8][9] Gantt charts are usually created initially using an early start time approach, where each task is scheduled to start immediately when its prerequisites are complete. This method maximizes the float time available for all tasks.[4] History [edit]

passages.text: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart that maps tasks, deadlines, and dependencies across a project timeline. Many Gantt charts also show milestones, owners, and progress alongside the dependencies that link tasks. These details help you understand who’s doing what, what needs to happen next, and which dates may be affected when work falls behind. For example, a website launch might include writing copy, designing pages, building the site, and testing it. A Gantt chart puts those tasks on one timeline, showing where work can happen together and where one task needs to finish before another begins. I’ll be honest: Gantt charts used to intimidate me. But once I started using them, I realized how much stress and guesswork they remove from planning. This guide explains how to read a Gantt chart, when to use one, and how to build a schedule your team can follow. How a Gantt chart works A Gantt chart turns your project into a visual timeline. Tasks span the dates when work happens, showing how long each one lasts and where it fits in the flow of your project. The horizontal layout makes it easy to understand sequence, timing, and workload at a glance.

The first known tool of this type was developed in 1896 by Karol Adamiecki, who called it a harmonogram.[10] Adamiecki, however, published his chart only in Russian and Polish which limited both its adoption and recognition of his authorship. In 1912, Hermann Schürch published what could be considered Gantt charts while discussing a construction project. Charts of the type published by Schürch appear to have been in common use in Germany at the time;[11][12][13] however, the prior development leading to Schürch's work is unclear.[14] Unlike later Gantt charts, Schürch's charts did not display interdependencies, leaving them to be inferred by the reader. Ask yourself: - What are we delivering, and what does “done” mean? - Is there a fixed deadline? - Who needs to contribute or approve the work? - What constraints could affect timing? For a website launch, “Publish the new site” is a starting point. Specifying the pages, required content, approvals, and launch conditions gives you something you can schedule. Capture those decisions in a short scope statement or project brief. Refer back to it when new requests arrive so you can discuss their effect on the timeline. When a simpler approach may fit better A task list or board may be enough when work is short, independent, and flexible about timing. If you’re collecting ideas or responding to incoming requests, maintaining a detailed schedule may add little value. Exploratory work needs particular care. When you don’t yet know the steps or outcomes, a detailed timeline can suggest more certainty than you have. You can still schedule a research window or decision milestone, then add detail as the work becomes clearer. Why use a Gantt chart for project management? A shared Gantt chart gives your team a place to check dates, responsibilities, and handoffs. Its value shows up in everyday decisions: what to start, who needs help, and what to change when a deadline is at risk.
